uses.reason: Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(4) is a statutory deeming rule for an ostensible business or professional partnership used to conceal subletting. The supplied case record concerns DTC/MCD and statutory succession or possession, with no alleged partner or sham partnership, so this subsection does not materially assist the fixed section 14(1)(b) issue.
uses.law_quote: allowed any person to occupy the whole or any part of the premises ostensibly on the ground that such person is a partner of the tenant

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage concerns permissive family occupation between persons living as husband and wife and warns against inferring a sublease from that relationship alone. Nothing in the supplied DTC/MCD record presents family occupation or a comparable domestic permissive-user relationship.
uses.law_quote: Sub-letting like letting, is a particular type of demise of immovable property and is distinct from permissive user like that of a licensee.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage applies Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(4) only to an ostensible partnership concealing real subletting. The supplied case contains no partnership theory, so the statutory deeming mechanism addressed here is outside the live DTC/MCD dispute.
uses.law_quote: the premises could be deemed to have been sub-let by the tenant only when the Controller is satisfied that some person is let into possession ostensibly as a partner in business but really for the purposes of sub-letting.

uses.reason: The Supreme Court's Delhi section 14 burden rule directly bears on the disputed possession evidence: the ARC recorded MCD in possession paying Rs.3500 to DTC, while respondents denied any parting and claimed MCD retained legal possession throughout. Its burden shift depends on prima facie proof of exclusive possession for consideration, so it helps evaluate those competing characterizations without deciding the ultimate ground.
uses.law_quote: the onus to prove sub-letting is on the landlord. If the landlord prima-facie shows that the occupant who was in exclusive possession of the premises let out for valuable consideration, it would then be for the tenant to rebut the evidence.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court synthesis arises under the Goa rent statute and in a partnership setting, so it is analogical rather than Delhi substantive law. Its retained-control principle is nevertheless useful context because the supplied case squarely disputes whether DTC parted with legal possession or whether possession remained with MCD throughout.
uses.law_quote: If tenant is actively associated with the partnership business and retains the control over the tenancy premises with him, may be along with partners, the tenant may not be said to have parted with possession.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage under the Goa rent statute addresses pleading and proof where a purported partnership may conceal subletting. The supplied DTC/MCD dispute alleges statutory transformation and contested possession, not a sham partnership or pleading variance of that kind.
uses.law_quote: the court may be required to tear the veil of partnership to find out the real nature of transaction entered into by the tenant

uses.reason: Although this is a Supreme Court synthesis under the Goa rent statute, its general exclusive-possession and burden-shifting principles materially illuminate the same factual dispute over MCD's possession and DTC's alleged loss of legal possession. The passage must be used with its stated limitation that compensation is part of its subletting formulation and should not be imported into every Delhi assignment or parting-with-possession alternative.
uses.law_quote: Initial burden of proving subletting is on landlord but once he is able to establish that a third party is in exclusive possession of the premises and that tenant has no legal possession of the tenanted premises, the onus shifts to tenant

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage arises under the Bombay rent statute and mainly tests whether a partnership is genuine, a mechanism absent here. Its narrower statement that subletting requires parting with legal possession provides qualified background to the DTC/MCD dispute over legal possession, but the partnership and Bombay-law portions are not controlling.
uses.law_quote: there cannot be a subletting, unless the lessee parted with legal possession.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court authority concerns the 1952 Delhi and Ajmer Act and a lease-versus-license inquiry, not the 1958 Delhi Act's exact section 14(1)(b) setting. Its treatment of exclusive possession as important but not conclusive, and of retained control as relevant, is useful by analogy to the disputed DTC/MCD possession evidence.
uses.law_quote: The test of exclusive possession, though not conclusive, is a very important indication in favour of tenancy

uses.reason: The Supreme Court's evidentiary rule under the 1952 Delhi and Ajmer Act is not the governing 1958 statute, but it materially assists the live proof issue because the supplied record contains findings of MCD possession and payment to DTC and a contrary claim that no parting occurred. Its force is limited to the stated prima facie combination of exclusive possession and valuable consideration, with withheld primary agreements being an additional fact in that authority.
uses.law_quote: The respondent discharged the onus by leading evidence showing that the occupants were in exclusive possession of the apartments for valuable consideration.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage under the predecessor Delhi and Ajmer rent statute directly helps define the written-consent issue by rejecting implied or temporally mismatched consent as sufficient for a particular subletting. That is material because the ARC recorded that no written consent was obtained, though the authority's statutory version and factual setting differ from the 1958 Act.
uses.law_quote: These letter,.; do not amount to a consent in writing to sub-lettings of portions of the hotel to the persons mentioned therein.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court authority applies Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b) to a regulatory-driven business transfer and holds that an actual assignment of leasehold rights without written consent falls within the clause. It is materially relevant to the High Court's statutory-transformation reasoning, but the supplied authority itself distinguishes a FERA-related consensual assignment from direct statutory vesting, so that factual and legal distinction must be preserved.
uses.law_quote: Her written consent is a pre-condition, as envisaged under sub-section (i)(b) of cite17†Section 14 which was not obtained.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage, applying Delhi section 14(1)(b) and quoting Parasram Harnand Rao, directly supplies the counterargument that the clause's assignment language can reach even a court-confirmed or assumed involuntary sale. It does not establish that direct nationalisation or statutory vesting in the supplied DTC/MCD history is the same mechanism, so that limitation remains essential to its use.
uses.law_quote:
The language of s.14(b) is wide enough not only to include any sub-
lease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court passage addresses independent sub-tenant protection under Delhi Rent Control Act sections 17 and 18, not the fixed section 14(1)(b) eviction ground. It still provides meaningful context that consent and notice must be evidenced by writing tied to the particular sub-tenancy, which bears on the record's assertion that no written consent existed.
uses.law_quote: The essence of the requirement, therefore, is that the consent of the landlord to the sub-tenancy and the notice of the creation of the sub-tenancy have to be evidenced by writing.

uses.reason: This is a concurring limitation concerning Delhi sections 17 and 18 and the exceptional protection of a sub-tenant, so it is not controlling on the fixed section 14(1)(b) ground. It offers only qualified context by stressing that written consent cannot normally be inferred from an incidental landlord signature and that the section 17 conditions are ordinarily strict.
uses.law_quote: I should not, therefore, be understood to hold the view that, as a general rule, in all cases where the sub-tenant some- how secures the signature of the land-lord in some communication relating to tenancy, a consent in writing satisfying the requirements of the section is to be assumed.

uses.reason: This Supreme Court authority concerns ordinary inheritance of a Delhi commercial tenancy after the tenant's death. The supplied dispute instead concerns corporate or public-body statutory transformations and alleged transfer of possession between DTC and MCD, and the authority itself does not address corporate amalgamation or statutory vesting.
uses.law_quote: commercial tenancies notwithstanding the determination of the contractual tenancies will devolve on the heirs in accordance with law
